title: “Selah” — what does the word tell the reader or singer?
summary: In the Psalms the word “Selah” first stands at the end of 3:2. It is printed 71 times in the KJV Psalms and three times in Habakkuk 3. The KJV leaves it as it is, and the verses quoted do not say what it means or what is to be done at it.
text: KJV Psalms 3:2: “Many there be which say of my soul, There is no help for him in God. Selah.” KJV 3:4: “I cried unto the Lord with my voice, and he heard me out of his holy hill. Selah.” KJV 3:8: “Salvation belongeth unto the Lord: thy blessing is upon thy people. Selah.” KJV Psalms 9:16: “The Lord is known by the judgment which he executeth: the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands. Higgaion. Selah.” KJV Habakkuk 3:3: “God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah.” Hebrew (WLC), numbered 3:3 because the title is counted as verse 1: אֵ֤ין יְֽשׁוּעָ֓תָה לֹּ֬ו בֵֽאלֹהִ֬ים סֶֽלָה. Brenton’s Greek, numbered 3:3: οὐκ ἔστι σωτηρία αὐτῷ ἐν τῷ Θεῷ αὐτοῦ· διάψαλμα. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/3/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA003.htm.
reasoning: In the verses quoted the word stands inside the text, after the end of a sentence, once beside another unexplained word (“Higgaion. Selah.”), and it is not part of the sentence it follows. Whether it is an instruction for music, a direction to the reader, or a word of the prayer itself decides whether it is to be read aloud as part of the psalm and how the psalm is divided. The KJV carries the Hebrew word over in English letters, and the verses quoted give it no explanation.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that it marks a pause or an interlude in the music; that it tells the singers to lift up the voice or the instruments; and that it is a word of assent or emphasis spoken with the psalm. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, in the KJV or in the Hebrew, and this record asserts none. The Greek quoted prints a different word, διάψαλμα, in the same place; this record does not say what that word means, and a rendering in another language is not an explanation given by the text. Check made: the packaged KJV was searched for the whole word “Selah”, case-sensitively. It is printed 75 times: 71 in the Psalms, 3 in Habakkuk 3, and once at 2 Kings 14:7, where it is the name of a place. The five verses quoted were read; the other verses were counted and not each read for an explanation. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. The Hebrew and the Greek run one verse ahead of the KJV in Psalm 3. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek quoted is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: “Thou shalt keep them, O Lord” — who or what is kept: the poor and needy, or the words of the Lord?
summary: Psalm 12:7 says the Lord will keep “them” and preserve “them” for ever. The verse before speaks of “the words of the Lord”, and the verse before that of the poor and the needy. The KJV verse does not say which it means.
text: KJV Psalms 12:5: “For the oppression of the poor, for the sighing of the needy, now will I arise, saith the Lord; I will set him in safety from him that puffeth at him.” KJV 12:6: “The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times.” KJV 12:7: “Thou shalt keep them, O Lord, thou shalt preserve them from this generation for ever.” KJV 12:1: “Help, Lord; for the godly man ceaseth; for the faithful fail from among the children of men.” KJV 12:8: “The wicked walk on every side, when the vilest men are exalted.” Hebrew (WLC), numbered 12:8: אַתָּֽה־יְהוָ֥ה תִּשְׁמְרֵ֑ם תִּצְּרֶ֓נּוּ ׀ מִן־הַדֹּ֖ור ז֣וּ לְעֹולָֽם. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/12/.
reasoning: What is promised depends on what “them” is. If it is the poor and needy of verse 5, the verse promises that people will be guarded from “this generation”. If it is the words of verse 6, the verse promises that the Lord’s words will be preserved for ever. The pronoun stands nearest to the words; the psalm opens with the godly man ceasing and closes with the wicked on every side.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The two outcomes named above are readings, not findings. Possible readings: that “them” is the poor and the needy of verse 5; that “them” is the words of the Lord of verse 6; and that the first “them” is one and the second the other. Each is an interpretation; the KJV verses quoted state none of them, and this record asserts none. In the Hebrew quoted the two verbs carry two different endings (the first ends in ם, the second in נו); this record does not say how either ending is to be read, and the Hebrew verse does not name what is kept either. A separate record compares the Greek, which has “us” in both places; a Greek rendering is one ancient reading of the verse, not a statement by the Hebrew or the KJV. The psalm is verse. Check made: all eight verses of Psalm 12 were read in the packaged KJV; no other psalm or book was searched for a statement about this verse. The Hebrew runs one verse ahead of the KJV in this psalm. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. title: “In the volume of the book it is written of me” — which book, and what is written there?
summary: The speaker of Psalm 40 says that something is written of him “in the volume of the book”. The verses quoted do not name the book or say what it has written. Hebrews 10:7 repeats the sentence and does not name the book either.
text: KJV Psalms 40:6: “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required.” KJV 40:7: “Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me,” KJV 40:8: “I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.” KJV Hebrews 10:5: “Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith” KJV Hebrews 10:7: “Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.” Hebrew (WLC), numbered 40:8: בִּמְגִלַּת־סֵ֝֗פֶר כָּת֥וּב עָלָֽי. Brenton’s Greek, numbered 39:8: ἐν κεφαλίδι βιβλίου γέγραπται περὶ ἐμοῦ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/40/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA039.htm.
reasoning: The speaker appeals to a writing as the ground of his coming (“Lo, I come”), set against sacrifice and offering. Which writing it is decides what he claims: that a law binds him as it binds others, or that a book speaks of him in particular. The phrase “the volume of the book” is printed only twice in the packaged KJV, here and where Hebrews repeats it.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Possible readings: that the book is the law, in which a duty is written for the speaker (verse 8 goes on, “thy law is within my heart”); that it is a writing that foretells the speaker; and that it is a record kept by God. Each is an interpretation; the verses quoted state none of them, and this record asserts none. Hebrews 10:5 brings the words in with “when he cometh into the world, he saith”, so Hebrews gives the words to the one it is speaking of there; the verses of Hebrews quoted repeat “the volume of the book” and do not say which book it is. The Hebrew and the Greek quoted have the same clause and name no book. A separate record compares the Greek of verse 6. The psalm is verse. Check made: Psalms 40:6–8 and Hebrews 10:5–7 were read in the packaged KJV, and the packaged KJV was searched for the phrase “volume of the book” (these two verses only). That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. Brenton’s Greek numbers this psalm 39, and the Hebrew and the Greek run one verse ahead of the KJV.
